title: Thermocouple Burnout Detection | Causes, Circuit and Industrial Importance
text:
Thermocouple Burnout: Introduction
 Thermocouples are among the most widely used temperature sensors in the process industry. You will find them in furnaces, boilers, reactors, kilns,  heat exchangers , and almost every high-temperature application. They are simple, rugged, and suitable for harsh environments.
 However, one common weakness of thermocouples is that they usually fail in an open-circuit condition . This failure is known as thermocouple burnout .
 If burnout is not detected properly, it can lead to false temperature readings, unstable control loops, and even unwanted plant trips. That is why thermocouple burnout detection is an essential feature in temperature instruments,  PLCs , and control systems.
 This article explains  thermocouple  burnout detection in a clear and practical way, covering how it works, why it is needed, and how instruments respond when a thermocouple fails.
 What Is Thermocouple Burnout? 
 A thermocouple consists of two dissimilar metals joined at one end , called the hot junction. When this junction is exposed to temperature, a small millivoltage is generated due to the Seebeck effect. The other ends are connected to the measuring instrument.
 Thermocouple burnout occurs when:
 The hot junction physically breaks

 One of the thermocouple wires opens

 The compensation cable becomes disconnected

 In all these cases, the thermocouple becomes an open circuit , and no valid temperature signal reaches the instrument.
 
 
 
 What Is Thermocouple Burnout Detection?
 Thermocouple burnout detection is a design feature in temperature instruments that forces the output to a known, predictable state when the thermocouple circuit opens.
 Instead of allowing random noise to dominate the input, the instrument deliberately drives the measurement either high or low to clearly indicate sensor failure.
 This controlled behavior is called burnout mode .
 Basic Principle of Burnout Detection Circuit
 A simple burnout detection circuit includes:
 A very high-value resistor (typically mega-ohms)

 A small internal voltage source

 A selectable switch for burnout direction

 The resistor is connected so that it has negligible effect during normal operation , but becomes effective when the thermocouple opens.
 Why Open Thermocouples Are Dangerous 
 Modern temperature instruments have very high input impedance . This means they draw almost no current from the thermocouple.
 When a thermocouple circuit opens:
 The instrument input becomes electrically “floating”

 Nearby electrical noise couples into the input

 Noise from motors, VFDs, heaters, and power cables appears as voltage

 The instrument interprets this noise as temperature

 As a result, the display may show:
 Rapidly fluctuating temperature

 Extremely high temperature

 Random unstable readings

 This false indication can mislead operators and control systems.
 
 
 
 Typical Causes of Thermocouple Burnout 
 Thermocouple burnout does not happen randomly. It usually occurs due to practical field conditions.
 Excessive process temperature When the hot junction is exposed to temperatures beyond its rated limit, the thermocouple materials oxidize or melt, leading to an open circuit.

 Mechanical damage Vibration, bending, or poor installation can cause the thermocouple wire to break over time.

 Compensation cable failure If the extension or compensation cable is cut, loose, or damaged, the circuit becomes open even if the sensor is intact.

 Hot work near cables Cutting, welding, grinding, or chipping near thermocouple cables can burn or damage insulation and conductors.

 Aging and corrosion Long exposure to high temperature and corrosive environments weakens thermocouple materials, eventually causing burnout.

 Consequences of Thermocouple Burnout
 When burnout is not detected, serious operational issues can occur.
 Erroneous temperature readings Electrical noise may appear as false temperature, causing incorrect process decisions.

 Unstable process control Temperature controllers may hunt or oscillate due to fluctuating inputs.

 Unwanted plant trips Safety logic may trip equipment based on false high or low temperature signals.

 Safety risks Operators may take wrong corrective actions based on incorrect temperature indication.

 Because of these risks, burnout detection is not optional—it is essential.
 
 
 
 High Burnout vs Low Burnout Selection
 The choice between high and low burnout depends on process safety philosophy.
 High burnout selection Used when a high temperature reading is safer, such as shutting down heaters or furnaces.

 Low burnout selection Used when a low temperature indication is safer, such as preventing cold-start damage.

 The SPDT switch or software configuration allows engineers to select the safest response.
 PLC and SCADA Integration
 Modern PLCs continuously monitor thermocouple input values.
 If the input suddenly goes beyond normal limits

 Or jumps to a configured burnout value

 The PLC recognizes it as thermocouple failure

 The PLC then:
 Generates a thermocouple burnout alarm

 Displays fault status on SCADA

 Allows maintenance teams to act quickly

 This prevents blind operation and improves plant reliability.
 What we learn today?
 Thermocouple burnout is a common and unavoidable failure mode in industrial environments. What matters is how the control system reacts when it happens .
 Thermocouple burnout detection ensures that when a sensor fails open, the instrument responds in a controlled, predictable, and safe manner. By forcing the signal high or low instead of allowing noise to dominate, burnout detection protects processes, equipment, and people.
 For any serious temperature measurement application, burnout detection is not just a feature—it is a necessity .
